teaser: One man spent 27 years on a single pair of doors. Florence gave them its best address.
review_notes:
The photo shows the doors in place on the east side of the Florence Baptistery, where a replica has hung since 1990; the originals are in the Museo dell'Opera del Duomo. Lesson says so explicitly.
Marble Baptism of Christ group above the door: begun by Andrea Sansovino in 1502, finished by others (angel added in the 18th century). Check.
Michelangelo's remark naming the doors comes from Vasari; presented as a reported story.
Ghiberti's first doors were moved from the east to the north side to make room: check.
Self-portrait head: located on the inner strip of the left door around mid-height; the spot is approximate because the heads are tiny in this photo and partly behind the fence.
Panels are small in this image: interactive blocks point only at whole panels, and those in the lower three rows are partly hidden by the railing.
Restoration lasted 27 years (finished 2012), six panels torn loose in the 1966 flood: check.

lesson.text: In the middle of Florence stands an eight-sided building clad in white and green marble: the Baptistery of San Giovanni. For centuries, every child born in the city was carried here to be baptized. Dante was one of them. It was the place where you became a Florentine.

The Baptistery has three doorways. The one in this photo is the east one, the door of honor, because it looks straight at the front of the cathedral a few steps away. Whatever hung here would be seen by every procession and every proud visitor. In 1425 the city decided it deserved something new.

lesson.title: The east doorway
lesson.text: Before the panels, see how the whole wall is arranged around them.

spots.title: A baptism in marble
spots.text: Above the door, John the Baptist pours water over Christ while an angel watches. The group was added in the 1500s, well after the doors. It tells you what the building is for.

spots.title: Ten golden squares
spots.text: Two leaves, five panels each. Every square is a bronze relief, a sculpture that rises from a flat background, covered in gold. The whole door stands about 5 meters (17 ft) tall.

spots.title: The dark frame
spots.text: Around the gold runs a frame of ungilded bronze, thick with leaves and fruit. Its darkness makes the panels glow brighter, like a picture frame chosen with care.

lesson.text: The job went to Lorenzo Ghiberti, and nobody else was even asked. He had earned that. In 1401, barely in his twenties, he had won a famous contest for an earlier pair of Baptistery doors, beating Filippo Brunelleschi, the future architect of the cathedral dome. Those first doors took him 21 years.

The second pair took 27 years, from 1425 to 1452. Add the first pair and Ghiberti gave nearly half a century to the doors of one building. He died in 1455, three years after the last panel was gilded.

A scholar had proposed 28 small scenes, like the older doors. Ghiberti chose ten big squares instead, each about 80 cm (31 in) wide, and all drawn from the Old Testament. Fewer frames, more room: each square holds several moments of one story at once.
The ten panels are read like a page of text. Tap the square where the story begins.

spots.title: Adam and Eve
spots.text: Top left, as on a page. In this one square Adam is created, Eve rises from his side, and both are driven out of the garden. Then the eye goes right, and down row by row.

lesson.text: Three episodes in one frame, with the same characters appearing several times: art historians call this continuous narrative. It sounds confusing, yet it works, because Ghiberti sorts the moments by depth. The main event stands out in front, and the earlier or later ones fade into the distance.

That depth is the real invention. Figures at the front are modeled almost fully round, close to breaking free of the bronze. Hills, trees and buildings behind them are barely raised, thin as a coin. Ghiberti also used linear perspective, the new method of making lines shrink toward a single point, so a few centimeters of metal read as a deep space.
Ghiberti made bronze behave like a painting: high relief up close, a whisper of relief far away, and perspective to hold it together.

The nickname is said to come from Michelangelo. According to the writer Vasari, he looked at the doors and declared them fit to be the gates of Paradise. The name stuck, helped by the fact that the space between a baptistery and its cathedral was already called a “paradiso.”

What shines in this photo is a faithful copy. In 1966 the river Arno flooded Florence and the water tore six panels from their frames. Pollution was also eating the gold. The originals came down in 1990 and were cleaned for 27 years, as long as they took to make. They now rest in a sealed case in the cathedral museum next door.

spots.title: Cain and Abel
spots.text: Top right. You can make out a slope and a team of oxen pulling a plow: Cain the farmer at work, before he kills his brother higher up in the same square.

spots.title: Noah
spots.text: Second row, left. Ghiberti gave the ark the shape of a pyramid, following an old scholarly idea, instead of the usual boat. Its sloping sides fill the back of the scene.

spots.title: Abraham
spots.text: Second row, right. Tall trees split the square in two. Below, Abraham welcomes three angels. Higher up, he is about to sacrifice his son Isaac.

spots.title: Jacob and Esau
spots.text: Third row, left, behind the railing. The round arches of a great hall are just visible. This panel is the showpiece of perspective: the floor and arches pull your eye deep into the bronze.

spots.title: Solomon and Sheba
spots.text: The last square, bottom right. Unlike the others, it shows one single moment: the meeting of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba in front of a temple, with a crowd watching.

spots.title: Small heads
spots.text: Between the panels, the gilded strips carry tiny statues of prophets and round medallions with heads. One of those heads, near the middle of the left door, is not a prophet at all.

lesson.text: That head is bald, with raised eyebrows and a half smile: Ghiberti himself, looking out at eye level from the door that used up his life. Nearby he signed it in Latin, stating that it was “made with marvelous art.” Standing where this photo was taken, with the cathedral at your back, it is hard to call that boasting.

quiz.question: Why was the east doorway of the Baptistery the most prestigious one?
options: It faces the front of the cathedral
It was reserved for the pope
quiz.explanation: The east door looks straight at the cathedral facade, so it was the door of honor.

quiz.question: How long did Ghiberti work on the Gates of Paradise?
quiz.explanation: He worked on them from 1425 to 1452.

quiz.question: Where does the story on the doors begin?
options: In the center, at eye level
Top left, with Adam and Eve
quiz.explanation: The panels read like a page: from the top left, left to right, row by row.

quiz.question: What does “continuous narrative” mean?
options: A story told by a guide in front of the work
Several moments of one story shown in a single frame
A series of panels with no frames between them
quiz.explanation: The same characters appear several times in one panel, at different moments.

quiz.question: How did Ghiberti create a sense of deep space in a few centimeters of bronze?
options: By raising foreground figures high and keeping the background very shallow
quiz.explanation: Strong relief in front, barely raised forms behind, plus perspective.

facts.text: The doors hanging on the Baptistery today are a copy.
facts.explanation: The originals were taken down in 1990 and are kept in the cathedral museum.

facts.text: Ghiberti followed the advice to divide the doors into 28 small scenes.
facts.explanation: He chose ten large square panels instead.

facts.text: Ghiberti put a portrait of himself on the doors.
facts.explanation: His bald head looks out from a medallion between the panels of the left door.
